## Week 5: functional structures

Five ways to shape a predictor, introduced together and compared on one task: ridge and the lasso (what a penalty changes, and what $\lambda$ controls), additive models (a spline as regression on basis functions, one curve per input), trees and random forests, and a neural network as a GLM of GLMs. Each has a knob, tuned on held-out data, with a test set opened once. Simulated data with three kinds of truth show that no structure wins everywhere, and the optimism theorem says why training error underestimates the risk of a fitted model. Data: Spotify tracks, what makes a song popular.

**Reading**

- ISLR Chapter 6 (Linear Model Selection and Regularization), sections 6.2.1–6.2.2, pp. 237–250: ridge regression and the lasso, and what each penalty does to the coefficients. Stop before 6.2.3.
- ISLR Chapter 7 (Moving Beyond Linearity), sections 7.3–7.4, pp. 294–301 (basis functions and regression splines), and section 7.7, pp. 306–310 (generalized additive models; 7.7.1 fits one by least squares on spline basis functions, as the lecture does, and the GAM part of the lab in 7.8 has the `lm` and `ns()` code). Skim 7.6, pp. 304–306 (local regression).
- ISLR Chapter 8 (Tree-Based Methods), section 8.1.1, pp. 328–335 (regression trees), and sections 8.2.1–8.2.2, pp. 340–345 (bagging and random forests). Skim 8.1.2–8.1.4, pp. 335–340.

Optional: PPA Chapter 6 (Generalization), "Generalization gap", pp. 100–101, the setting of the optimism theorem.
